extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (personal identity and moral theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes normative criteria and conceptual definitions Locke advances about personal identity, selfhood, responsibility, and classifications of relations and moral rules. Useful for philosophical analysis, teaching, or applying Locke's standards to thought-experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal identity consists in identity of consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Personal identity is preserved’ where the same consciousness is preserved; personal identity ‘reaching no further than consciousness reaches.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke repeatedly asserts that sameness of person is constituted by continuity or sameness of consciousness (memory, awareness) rather than by sameness of substance or body. Examples: if the same consciousness that saw Noah’s flood were present now, the same self would be identified across those events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness, not numerical substance or bodily sameness, grounds selfhood
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘SELF is that conscious thinking thing… whatever substance made up of… which is sensible or conscious of pleasure and pain… and so is concerned for itself, as far as that consciousness extends.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'self' is defined as the conscious thinking thing irrespective of material or immaterial substrate. Locke uses thought experiments (e.g., consciousness following a cut-off little finger) to show that what matters is what consciousness is aware of, not the underlying substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same immaterial substance without memory does not make the same person
rubrics_metrics.description: If an immaterial being is ‘wholly stripped of all the consciousness of its past existence’ it will make different persons despite being the same immaterial substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to doctrines of pre-existence or transmigration: mere numerical sameness of an immaterial soul does not preserve personal identity if consciousness of past actions is absent. Locke’s Pythagorean examples show that absence of memory/seeming awareness separates persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: The body, as well as the soul, goes to making a man (distinction: man vs person)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the same soul carrying its consciousness into another body could make the same PERSON, the same SOUL alone ‘would scarce to any one but to him that makes the soul the man, be enough to make the same man.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke distinguishes ‘man’ (a human individual often tied to bodily continuity) from ‘person’ (tied to consciousness). One can be the same person across different bodies if consciousness continues, but the label ‘man’ typically invokes bodily or composite criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness unites actions into the same person over time
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Consciousness… unites existences and actions very remote in time into the same PERSON, as well as it does the existences and actions of the immediately preceding moment.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity of awareness or memory permits a single person to appropriate past actions; Locke applies this to notions of resurrection and to moral/accountability considerations (one is accountable for those actions one can appropriate by consciousness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self is concerned for itself only insofar as consciousness extends
rubrics_metrics.description: What is ‘himself’ is the part apprehended by present consciousness; whatever consciousness goes with (even a small limb, in Locke’s example) would be the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative example: if consciousness were to go with a detached finger, that finger would be the person. The scope of self-interest, responsibility, and moral concern tracks the scope of consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons, not substances, are proper objects of reward and punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In this personal identity is founded all the right and justice of reward and punishment… happiness and misery being that for which every one is concerned for HIMSELF.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral and legal responsibility should attach to the person defined by consciousness. Punishing a subject for actions of which their present consciousness cannot appropriate would be unjust, according to Locke’s argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute oblivion separates forgotten actions from the person (but not from the man)
rubrics_metrics.description: If someone wholly loses memory of parts of their life beyond retrieval, those past actions are separated from the present PERSON even if the same MAN remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke distinguishes forensic/accountability relevance (personhood via consciousness) from biological/historical identity (man). Legal and moral practice (e.g., not punishing the mad for the sober man’s actions) reflects this distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of man vs person: three senses of ‘same man’ but personal identity only by consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Three possible senses of 'the same man': (1) same individual immaterial thinking substance; (2) same animal; (3) same immaterial spirit united to same animal. Yet personal identity cannot consist in anything but consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes that depending on which sense of 'man' one adopts, different puzzles arise, but insists that whichever account is chosen, personal identity must ultimately be tied to consciousness to avoid absurdities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human legal practice treats altered-consciousness cases pragmatically; divine judgment will follow actual consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Human laws punish drunken or sleepwalking persons because society cannot distinguish reality from counterfeit, but on the 'Great Day' no one shall be made to answer for what he knows nothing of; divine judgment will follow consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes pragmatic legal policy (where courts hold people responsible despite ignorance) from metaphysical/moral ideal (where responsibility requires conscious appropriation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Only consciousness can unite remote existences into one person (thought-experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two incommunicable consciousnesses act the same body at day and night, they would be two persons; conversely the same consciousness acting in two bodies would make one person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke’s thought-experiments (day/night split consciousness; same consciousness in two bodies) illustrate that identity-tracking must rest on persistence of consciousness, not on continuity of substance or bodily continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness determines identity regardless of the particular substance it is united with
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Whatsoever any substance has thought or done, which I cannot recollect, and by my consciousness make my own thought and action, it will no more belong to me…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an immaterial soul or material particles are numerically the same across time, without conscious appropriation their past is not mine; consciousness is the unifying principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness can unite material or spiritual substances into the same personality
rubrics_metrics.description: The same continued consciousness may have united several substances at different times such that various substances were parts of the same self while vitally united to that consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke allows for the same numerical substance becoming part of different persons across time if consciousness does not appropriate past actions, and conversely different substances forming one person when consciousness persists across them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person is a forensic term for agents capable of law, reward, and punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘PERSON… is the name for this self… It is a forensic term, appropriating actions and their merit; and so belongs only to intelligent agents, capable of a law, and happiness, and misery.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the conceptual role of 'person' as tied to moral and legal assessment; emphasizes that attribution of praise/blame depends on identifying the conscious agent that can own past actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral good and evil defined as conformity or disagreement of voluntary actions to a law
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘MORAL GOOD AND EVIL… is only THE CONFORMITY OR DISAGREEMENT OF OUR VOLUNTARY ACTIONS TO SOME LAW, WHEREBY GOOD OR EVIL IS DRAWN ON US, FROM THE WILL AND POWER OF THE LAW-MAKER.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke grounds moral evaluation in obedience or disobedience to a rule that carries sanctioned rewards or punishments (not merely natural consequences). Voluntariness of action is essential to moral status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral rules must have enforcement (rewards/punishments) beyond natural consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule set to the free actions of men must have some enforcement of good and evil by the law-maker; otherwise the rule would be vain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke emphasizes that law (properly so called) presupposes the power to reward/punish in ways that are not mere natural consequences of actions; this distinguishes moral/legal norms from neutral descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three sorts of laws/judgment: divine, civil, and opinion/reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws men generally refer their actions to are: (1) DIVINE law (measure of sin and duty), (2) CIVIL law (measure of crimes and innocence), (3) LAW OF OPINION OR REPUTATION (measure of virtue and vice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each law has its own sanctions and domain: divine law concerns ultimate happiness/misery; civil law concerns punishments administered by the commonwealth; opinion regulates praise/disgrace in society. Moral appraisal depends on which rule is being applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divine law is the touchstone of moral rectitude (sin and duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: By comparison to the DIVINE LAW men judge of the most considerable moral good or evil of their actions; it is the only true touchstone of moral rectitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that divine law, backed by the power of the Almighty to reward or punish infinitely, provides the ultimate moral standard beyond civil statutes or reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil law measures crimes and innocence by the commonwealth’s rules and sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: CIVIL LAW… is the rule set by the commonwealth to the actions of those who belong to it… the force of the Commonwealth… engaged to protect the lives, liberties, and possessions of those who live according to its laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil law’s relevance rests on the commonwealth’s ability to apply proximate sanctions (loss of life, liberty, goods) and thus define criminality within a polity, distinct from divine or reputational judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of opinion (reputation) is the common measure of virtue and vice
rubrics_metrics.description: VIRTUE and VICE… are constantly attributed to such actions as in each country and society are in reputation or discredit… virtue is everywhere, that which is thought praiseworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social approbation and blame constitute the practical measure of virtue and vice in societies; Locke notes variation between cultures but argues that public esteem often aligns with natural right as enforced by divine law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of relations: proportional, natural, instituted (voluntary), and moral
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations of things include: proportional (comparisons of degree), natural (origin/birth relations like father/son), instituted/voluntary (relations from human conventions, e.g., general/army), and moral relations (conformity to rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke provides a taxonomy of relation-types to show different grounds on which things are compared or referred; moral relations are singled out as especially important because they determine moral appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common practical measure of virtue/vice is public esteem (practical standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘That this is the common MEASURE of virtue and vice, will appear… virtue is everywhere, that which is thought praiseworthy…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains why societies equate virtue with what is praised (and vice with what is blamed), arguing that public approbation tends generally to correspond with the rule of right grounded in divine law, even if local variations exist.
